comments.author: schmichael
comments.text: The weird thing about this product is that its biggest competitor is "an old ipad." I feel like most of their target customer base already has an old ipad that's better suited for what this does in every way. Old ipads: 1. Have a battery so you're not tied to a cord. Even old poor batteries are better than no battery. 2. Have apps! How does this not support apps?! 3. Have a huge range of 3rd party products and hacks and 3D models to wall mount it or stands for it 4. Are kitchen-safe (splatter proof, far fewer holes than this product, movable out of the way) 5. Also support siri and facetime and everything this device does AFAICT I'm guessing they realized this and made sure it's priced lower than the cheapest new iPad, but it will be interesting to see if the price difference can compete with the old iPads most of their customers have in drawers or already on walls. Maybe the purpose-built nature will be a reasonable enough differentiator, but I'm not sure it's focused enough for that. It's both a passive information station and for calls? It's for recipes which implies you put it in the kitchen, but it looks like a nightmare to clean with all those holes? It's also a very small screen when you have to read the recipe from a distance because it has no battery. I can't move my stove to it, and I definitely don't want it too near a stove or sink! The multiple users feature is a really neat trick, but I would kill to have this for all Apple devices. Let me hand my kid my phone and it automatically switches to kid mode! Please Apple don't lock multiple users to stationary devices like HomeView!

stories.title_en: Ledger confirms spy chip implant behind wallet crypto thefts
stories.title_ja: Ledgerがウォレット暗号通貨盗難の背後にスパイチップ埋め込みを確認

comments.author: TacticalCoder
comments.text: No matter whether you like or hate or don't care about cryptocurrencies, this is incredible stuff... Now basically: every single attack that's been described as "theoretical" or "far-fetched" or "only existing in the mind of a paranoid person" did actually happen. We're talking here about a tiny eSIM implant and a little CPU doing OCR on the fonts appearing on the hardware wallet's screen to read the secrets during set up. So the secure element ain't tampered with. Not long ago the Coldcard hardware wallet had an issue where it'd fallback to a 32-bit only RNG that could be cracked and so many people got their coins stolen. Now it's Ledger that sees tampered devices all around the world (in Asia for sure but now there are reports about reseller in the EU selling backdoored/eSIM'ed devices). For people who own Bitcoin at this point one of the only thing kinda sensible to do is to use multisig schemes, like 2-of-2 or 3-of-3 multisig, where your split the secret over two or three different hardware wallet brands (meaning being able to sign a 2-of-2 wallets requires hardware wallets from two different vendors). When Ledger hardware wallets came out and people said that seed (the list of words) could be intercepted and relayed by a channel bypassing the computer (here by using an eSIM), people would post explaining that people were nuts if they thought such an attack could be pulled off. Yet here we are. And Ledger is responsible for very poor security practices: for example it's impossible to use a Ledger hardware wallet in a fully airgapped/offline way. For you're forced to not only upgrade the firmware but also install the Bitcoin "ledger app" (or whatever that is called) after you entered your seed into the device. Which is complete and total amateur hour. In addition to that Ledger offers a service to "backup your seed": what could possibly go wrong with that uh? I'm betting that we'll soon hear about hardware wallets getting drained due to the seed being exfiltrated through "randomness" in how transactions are built/signed (aka "kleptography"). And it's not just representative about people in the cryptocurrencies ecosystem: people simply don't understand computer security and don't understand the potential attacks nor the length at which attackers are willing to go to steal data/funds/ruin other people's lives. At this point we've heard about chips' plans being modified before the chips are even built (only to lower the entropy of RNGs) [unrelated to cryptocurrencies btw], a worldwide backdoor attempt in SSH, eSIM sending secrets from hardware wallets with tiny attack surfaces. You're not anywhere near paranoid enough.

賛否両論については、攻撃の ingenuity を称賛する声と、Ledgerがファームウェアアップデートや公式アプリのインストールを強制し、シードのバックアップサービスを提供するなどセキュリティ意識が低いと批判する意見が分かれた。さらに、ハードウェアウォレットだけでは自己保管は不十分であり、マルチシグや異なるベンダー間での鍵分散が必要だと指摘するコメントも多かった。  
注目コメントとして、ドイツの大手量販店MediaMarktが店頭で改ざんデバイスを販売していたという事実を指摘したものや、「政府がやらない仕事をハッカーがやった」と賞賛する声、そして「ハードウェアウォレットは自動的に安全ではない、攻撃ポイントは多数存在する」と警鐘を鳴らす意見が特に洞察に富んでいたとされた。

stories.title_en: 11 year old unsoundness bugs found in Rust borrow checker

comments.author: GrantMoyer
comments.text: It's surprising this bug went unnoticed for so long, but at least it's easy to fix, since it's not a bug with the type system itself; it's just a bug in the compiler. The compiler should always have been rejecting that code according to lifetime rules of Rust's type system, so the fix is to just make it reject the code, rather than having to change the fundamental rules of lifetimes.

comments.author: weinzierl

comments.author: mrkeen
comments.text: Type systems are hard! Check out https://counterexamples.org/ I gave it a quick scan for Rust examples; there are 11 samples among the following pages: https://counterexamples.org/eventually-nothing.html https://counterexamples.org/mutable-matching.html https://counterexamples.org/selfishness.html https://counterexamples.org/scope-escape.html https://counterexamples.org/nearly-universal.html The first thing I always look for is mutability ( combined with some other tricky feature), e.g. "Now it's a Just(3):Maybe<Int> , now it's a Nothing:Maybe<Int> , now it's a Nothing:Maybe<String> ." stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、Rustの借用チェッカーに11年間見逃されていたunsoundなバグが型システムルールに違反しているにもかかわらずコンパイラの実装ミスだったことへの驚きと、修正は型システム変更ではなくコンパイラのチェックを厳しくするだけで済む点。賛否は、実際のクレートへの影響が不明で修正によりビルドできなくなるリスクを懸念する声と、型システムの信頼性向上のため早期修正を歓迎する声に分かれた。注目コメントでは、現在未解決のunsound問題が100以上あり、新しいtraitソルバーが一部の解決を助けるが今回のバグは対象外かもしれないこと、そしてAIによるコンパイラバグ探索が最終的に形式検証されたコンパイラへと導く可能性を指摘していた。
stories.editor_note: Rustのborrow checkerで発見された11年古い不健全性バグは、型システムの信頼性に影を落とすが、修正パッチが早くも提供され、日本の組み込み・金融系プロジェクトでの安全性再評価が進んでいる。

stories.title_en: A plea not to use uv-build

comments.author: woodruffw
comments.text: To copy my response on Lobsters: (I am one of uv’s maintainers.) The nice thing about Python packaging is that it’s standardized: if uv’s build backend doesn’t fit into the hole you want, then you can use any number of other backends that do an admirable job of conforming to the packaging standards. With that said, I don’t understand why Gentoo needs to rebuild every single release of uv-build. It doesn’t change as much as uv itself, and it’s intentionally compatible across uv versions. Why not set a policy of only updating once weekly, or even less frequently, with exceptions for important breaking changes or bug fixes? (For context: the only reason uv-build releases as often as it does is because it’s easier to keep its internals in lockstep with the rest of uv. But you can do a normal version bound in your Python build backend metadata and uv will happily use whatever version of uv-build is already present.)

They can request, and they do request nicely, but they also present the drawbacks for them as if they are absolute, and even claim that "its benefits don’t outweigh the drawbacks".

comments.author: shadowgovt
comments.text: I don't think I agree with the author's assessment here: > The other reason is performance and that argument makes even less sense. Even if it mattered, we’re realistically talking about a difference in the ballpark of 100 ms, for an action executed rarely; it is equally possible that any gain will be outweighed by the time needed to fetch the 1.5 MiB wheel for uv-build. Modern CI architectures are building Docker stacks from scratch and using a readthrough cache of wheels. Downloading may still be the dominant factor, but the second-dominant factor does start to add up, especially when the downloading gets cached at various layers.

comments.author: switz
comments.text: There is so much spam, abuse, and aggressive scraping that I've had to block: - AWS - Google Cloud - Azure - Alibaba Cloud - Oracle and a handful of other ASNs on almost all of my properties. It would be one thing if it was simple scraping, but it's often genuine agentic abuse (just spamming for vulnerabilities* or scraping millions of pages with very little valuable or dynamic content). These clouds must get the abuse happening under their own roof under control. I banned Alibaba's Cloud two years ago and it still hits one of my domains 1 million times per day, despite every route 4xx-ing during that time. Even Apple has aggressively ramped up its scraping in the past few months, but thankfully they do respect robots.txt. It's frustrating because some of my real users route through these clouds via their work VPNs. Also, there are a lot of less-than-reputable AI scrapers using global bot-nets via residential IPs to scrape, making it even harder to detect and ban them without affecting real people. * like leaked .env routes, brute forcing admin panels, and so on

stories.editor_note: HN投稿後、AIボットによるトラフィック急増は、スクレイピング防止のためのレートリミットやBot管理の重要性を改めて示す。日本のメディアサイトでも同様の対策が急がれ、WAF導入が加速している。

comments.author: solatic
comments.text: Folks here don't understand how big of a market this is. Island just raised a $400 million Series F at $6.4 billion valuation: https://www.island.io/press/island-announces-400-million-ser... Mozilla is also very, very far behind in this race. But the potential is real. Enterprises have both the budget and the motivation to care about DLP (including preventing employees from copy/pasting sensitive data into AI chat apps), VPN-less access to private intranet apps (including to contractors on BYOD), preventing access to sites that distract employees and have zero business value (pornography, gambling, etc.)... If you care about an open web browser, you should care about it having a sustainable revenue model. Enterprise browsers are exactly that revenue model . The question is not whether this is a good idea; the question is whether Mozilla can catch up.

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、EmbeddingGemma 2を音声からテキストへ変換する実験と、その結果得られた速度と精度、さらにオープンソース化への期待です。投稿者は音声とテキストが共有するベクトル空間を利用し、数日間の hack で WER が許容範囲内になるモデルを作り、クラウドモデルほどではないが日常利用に十分だと主張しています。これに対し、いくつかのコメントではモデルをCoreMLに変換し、macOSのNeural Engineで実行すると推論時間が60秒から10秒に短縮され、Swiftに依存なく移植すれば非技術者にも配布できるという具体的な高速化テクニックが紹介され、WhisperやDemucsなどのほかのモデルでも同様に効果があったと報じられています。また、別のユーザーはParakeet v3とMacWhisperをM1 MacBook Airで試し、クリック直後には転写が終わるほどの驚異的な速度を体験し、Appleのオンデバイス転写モデルは報告より約3倍遅いもののエラー率は許容範囲だと指摘しています。全体として、音声認識のローカル実行が劇的に速くなったことへの驚きと、精度向上のためのさらなる学習データやオープンソース公開への期待が議論の中心でした。

comments.author: comandillos

comments.author: martythemaniak
comments.text: I'm a robotics noob currently building a prototype of a snow sweeping robot (www.frost-e.com) using my own design and I'm encouraged to see similar work coming from real places. Namely: - Zero shot control using a visual harness and action primitives. I've seen this from a few other places as well ( https://tml.stanford.edu/homebody/ ) and it's essentially having a generalist LLM command a robot via a set of predefined actions. Many robots and many tasks can probably be done with this approach, since not everything needs super intricate 6DoF arms or dexterity - simulation bring-ups: I have a pipeline that takes in satellite imagery and reconstructs the lots and houses in a 3D environment and snows on it so that my virtual robot can learn to clean. With these latest models, you can probably create a higher fidelity digital twin more directly. - self-improvement: These models (Argon, Astra, etc) can't operate the robot itself, but would be able to create data to distill into smaller models you can actually utilize.

I mean - I guess we're maybe 5-7 years away from a reasonably priced robot you could plug into the wall like an old vacuum cleaner (that runs on this type of tech).

comments.author: munch-o-man
comments.text: I like the technical fun of it, but no musician is ever going to give a crap about this. We have hundreds of years of the evolution of music notation and it is pretty comprehensive. Just because there are only 12 unique notes in western music doesn't mean base-12 to notate it makes sense....that completely strips out context of what you are playing. For example...in the key of aminor when you make the five chord major to create a resolution back to i (aminor) you raise the 7th scale degree. That means the G becomes G#...Ab is the same pitch but writing it that way is wrong. An EMajor chord is spelled E G# B, not E Ab B. Now if you spell that as 9 0 4 you have stripped all context out of the music. Musicians aren't just player pianos, they analyze the harmonic structure of the music the inform phrasing, shape, tone, volume, and pacing (acelarando, decelerando, ritardando, etc). Whenever I see something like this trying to reinvent standard notation I feel like it is usually from somebody who can kind of play an instrument but can't read music or can't read it well because they haven't put the years of work it takes to be a proficient sight reader and they haven't studied harmony/music-theory. One of the most important things about musical standard notation is that it is - standard - you can hand it to any musician on any instrument and they can make sense of it quickly. It is a skill that takes a lot of practice but it is what allows musicians who have never met each other to be hired for a gig and show up and play together without ever rehearsing. This approach won't teach you to "see" music either. It forces pure mechanical number memory....you won't see harmony and be able to quickly notice that - for example - a line is just moving the chord up in inversions and since you know harmony and your chords you can sight read that part without ever even reading every individual note. But still a cool idea from a hobby perspective.

Dont burden the reader. Edit: I read the first half of the article then skimmed the rest (I dont use LLMs outside of occasional searches). I've been a gamedev for five years. I have a hunch LLMs will not take over game development because of the necessity to control many, many small details to shape a great experience for the player, and because some parts of development cannot be described with words. Small details: My hunch is when it comes time to polish and fine tune all the moving parts, this process will remain much faster to do by hand. It will be faster to update a specific field or line of code and test/iterate than to prompt your way through that process (the last 20% of the work takes 80% of the time) Describing without words: An artist with a vision can only bring that vision to life with body movements. It is not possible to communicate all the details that go into a great piece of art with words. The colors, lines, shapes, positioning, specific emotions, history... is beyond spoken language.

comments.author: bob1029
comments.text: > I stand by a lot of what I’ve said, but am in the process of shipping a project where I’ve also used none of this. I think the scale I’m targeting here is really larger projects. The author appears to be on track to learn an important lesson about LLMs and art. LLMs have completely solved the coding side of game development. But this was never the hard part. Not even close. The fixed randomness and determinism thing sounds great on paper (all of this does), but in reality this is an extremely confining way to build a video game. Ensuring you maintain determinism across many platforms is where things get super nasty. If you want a turnkey AI game development experience, why not double down on diffusion? This sidesteps virtually all of the tooling and integration concerns. There is no game engine to integrate with if you use a diffusion model.

comments.text: Just like writing, the biggest threat to game development isn't the LLMs themselves, but a failure to disclose LLM usage. Humans want to read things humans wrote, and humans want to play what humans made.

comments.author: theptip
comments.text: This matches what I came up with on a small project. The biggest ones being screenshots and separated simulation. Meta level, just push your agent to make things more legible, it’ll figure it out. One other observation, remember that your agent is infinitely patient. So prompts like “build an interactive design doc with videos of each game mechanic in the style of Factorio dev diaries” can make reviewing changes easier. The general idea, all the small QoL dev tools that you don’t have time for, you can just spawn a side agent to build; if they are orthogonal to your main thread you can just progress them in the background. One thing I think game dev has not (AFAIK) invested as much in is observability. There’s a lot of perf instrumentation available in debug builds, but things like measuring DPS, health, etc as an exported metric time series I have not seen before. I think agents will benefit from this disproportionately more than humans, eg for inspecting progression curves and balance.

stories.title_en: Show HN: Stream live open data in two commands
stories.title_ja: Show HN: 2つのコマンドでライブオープンデータをストリーム

comments.author: gardensalad
comments.text: Some more technical details. CLI The CLI is written in Go. Interpreted/VM approaches (specifically Python/Java) felt more involved (particularly at install time) for what was intended to be a lightweight, easy to install utility. Being able to output executable binaries was really important, and the high level language looked nice (I'm new to Go). There's no library (yet) - it's a CLI tool. My thinking is that a lot of the file management functionality has to talk to the file system (gigabyte files are technically doable, currently capped at 100MB while we work out the issues). The more I thought about adding multiple programming languages and flexible (stream to file, to string, to byte array) interfaces, the harder to use it looked; offloading concerns like memory usage and hash verification to the developer. With that said, there will be an API (I'm working on it now), and it'll have all the capabilities/interfaces of the CLI, but obviously be a roll-your-own logic situation. On the CLI, I really like how minimal the integration is - you write one file poller (examples in the docs) and you're basically done with the "get the data" problem and onto the more interesting "use the data" problem. It is a bit of an unusual approach though. I'm considering adding a callback command to the CLI that triggers after each payload is written, that would make integration even simpler and help scripts trigger appropriately. API The clients (just the CLI at the moment) subscribe to a websocket to listen to files being published (one for each subscription). This is the one technical decision that took me the most time. Long poll / regular poll were both considered and discarded due to the fairly heavy impact it has on LB billing when scaled out, particularly for heavy clients with high frequency polls. Directly exposing a Kafka queue had its own issues, and would have pushed the architecture to be a shape I wasn't a fan of for a public service (less auth control, looser control of server balancing, client version tie-in, etc). Downloads are via a signed link - this allows us to control access to the CDN and prevent us being flooded with requests from a given IP or account. I'm solo and self-funded so controlling spend is critical for us at the moment. Validation We do some basic checks for XML and JSON (e.g. XXE and other attacks) in all published files and we'll build up more checks and more data types over time. No file is visible to subscribers until it has passed validation. What's planned Priority 1 is on-boarding publishers so we have useful data on the site. General polish is high on the list (anything UX or DX - CLI, API, site usability) I have a few plans for different types of stream - high speed feeds being the main one. Supporting emerging (schema) standards is a consideration too (e.g. a community authored schema repository, being able to search by schema for similar data types)

stories.summary_ja: 主な議論点は、CLIをGoで実装しバイナリ配布によりインストールが簡単で軽量であること、現在はライブラリを提供せずAPIのみを将来的に用意するという点です。作者はPythonやJavaではインストール時のオーバーヘッドが大きく、Goの静的リンクバイナリが求める軽量さに合うと説明しています。複数言語サポートや柔軟なストリーム先を追加すると使い勝手が悪化し、メモリやハッシュ検証などの懸念を開発者に委ねるため、最小限のポーラー実装に留めています。賛否については、バイナリによる導入のしやすさとコスト削減への賛同が多い反面、言語の選択肢が狭く高度なカスタマイズが必要なユーザーには不便という意見もあります。注目ポイントとして、WebSocketを選んだのはロードバランサー費用と運用コントロールで優位であり、ペイロード書き込み後に呼び出せるコールバックコマンドを検討中です。

stories.title_en: Hittite royal archive found in Turkey

comments.author: schleck8
comments.text: The Hittites were one of the largest empires in the ancient world, but up until the last two centuries, the only proper documentation of them was in the Bible, which is why many historians suspected that they were a fictional civilization. In 1834, French archaelogist Texier found the ruins of their capital Hattusa in modern day Turkey. But he assumed it was Pteria, a city mentioned in ancient Greek documents. It took another ~ 70 years for German archaelogist Winckler to realize that this was the Hittite capital, based on clay tablets.

comments.author: flowerthoughts

Nice time machine you've got there. Not just vases and bones, but thoughts and societal complexities.

comments.author: sherr

comments.author: simonh
comments.text: We have some copies of royal correspondence found in Egypt, written on cuneiform tablets. They used them for messages to foreign kings because they're compact and durable. A lot of the surviving tablets are begging letters asking the Egyptians for gold. We even have some practice tablets from teaching Egyptian scribes to do this. Anyway I think some of these documents are of communications with Hittite kings, so it would be great to get some instances of the "other side" of some of these letters.

stories.summary_ja:
主な議論点: 新たに発見された131枚の楔形文字板が記録する疫病、軍事物流、宗教儀式、王族の日常生活など、遺物だけでは分からないヒッタイト人の思想や社会構造を直接知る手がかりとなったこと。また、エジプト出土のヒッタイト王宛て書簡とその「もう一方の側」を求める声、そしてヒッタイト語彙とインド・ヨーロッパ語族との関係解明への期待が示された。  
賛否両論: 多くのコメントはこの発見の重要性を称賛しているが、一部ではエジプト側の文書だけではヒッタイト側の視点が偏りやすいと指摘し、ヒッタイト側の資料が乏しいことへの懸念も見られた。ただし、今回の板が発見によってその偏りを補うとの期待が強い。  
注目コメント: 「Nice time machine you've got there.」という言葉で、板から得られる思想的側面に感嘆した声。「The History Blog is a small gem…」と信頼できる情報源として挙げられた点。さらに、「begging letters … would be great to get some instances of the 'other side'」と、エジプト側の請求文書に対しヒッタイト側の書簡を望む意見が特に目を引いた。
stories.editor_note: トルコでヒッタイト王家のアーカイブが発見されたことは、古代近東の行政文書理解に新たな素料を提供し、歴史学の研究手法を変える可能性がある。日本の東洋史研究者でもデジタルアーカイブ化への協力が期待される。
